tagline: A paved river corridor linking Yellowstone with early lodges and forest management
intro: The Buffalo Bill Cody Scenic Byway follows the North Fork of the Shoshone River through the Wapiti Valley to Yellowstone’s East Entrance. Travel Wyoming gives the paved U.S. 14/16/20 drive as 27 miles, taking approximately 45 minutes from the Shoshone National Forest boundary. Designated a National Forest Scenic Byway in 1991 and a Wyoming State Scenic Byway in 1995, it offers rock formations, wildlife and recreation highlighted by the Federal Highway Administration. Elk, grizzly bears, bighorn sheep, moose and deer inhabit the valley’s streamsides, grassy benches and brushy slopes.

The corridor’s early tourist trade left a landmark at Pahaska Tepee. Buffalo Bill Cody built the lodge for travelers taking the Cody Road to Yellowstone, and construction was completed in 1905. Forest administration was taking shape nearby: enlargement of the Shoshone forest required its division, and W. H. Pierce built the Wapiti Ranger Station in 1903 to administer the Shoshone division.

Driving east from Yellowstone’s East Entrance toward Cody, Pahaska Tepee comes first, two miles from the park. Farther down the North Fork, Mummy Cave occupies a volcanic cliff beside the highway. Next comes Wapiti Ranger Station, on the highway’s north side, before the drive reaches the forest boundary about 25 miles west of Cody.

moments.title: Pahaska Tepee
moments.text: Pahaska Tepee faces east, down the Shoshone River valley, with porches wrapping three sides of its two-story log structure. Buffalo Bill Cody built it to accommodate tourists heading for Yellowstone on the Cody Road. Artist Abraham Archibald Anderson designed the lodge in 1902 or 1903. Inside, the entrance hall rises to the roof, with mezzanine galleries and a stone fireplace at its far end. Cody used a small suite above the east porch. The building also changed after Cody’s time: a kitchen and dining-room addition erected in 1920 was demolished in 1962.

moments.title: Mummy Cave
moments.text: Mummy Cave is a broad, shallow rock shelter in a volcanic cliff beside the North Fork. Its dry deposits preserved hide, feathers and wood alongside stone artifacts. Excavations by the Buffalo Bill Historical Center exposed cultural deposits more than 28 feet deep, divided into 38 occupation levels. The shelter contains evidence of use between 7280 BC and AD 1580. The sequence of stone projectile points helped researchers classify arrowheads and spearheads from other Rocky Mountain sites. The cliff above has no vertical joints, and its pointed shape keeps rain and meltwater from seeping into the shelter.

moments.title: Wapiti Ranger Station
moments.text: A rail fence sets Wapiti’s original ranger station apart from the newer Forest Service buildings surrounding it. W. H. Pierce built the station in 1903, using native forest timber. It was the first Forest Service ranger station built with federal funding. The single-story log building has a low-pitched gabled roof; later rear extensions gave it a U-shaped plan. Its interior has been modernized, and the station continues to serve forest management. The forest’s expansion had required an administrative division; Pierce was the first administrator of its Shoshone division. Repairs in 2005 replaced rotting timber.
moments.notice: A rail fence separates the original log station from its newer neighbors.

practical: Pahaska Tepee: The byway is open year round; Yellowstone’s East Entrance closes the first Monday of November. (checked 2026-10-11)
